# Chapter XXV: Examination of Nirvana

In this regard, non-existence—or impermanence—is designated in dependence upon existence, for we do not observe the impermanence of a rabbit's horns. The object to be defined is designated depending on the definition, and the definition is designated depending on the object. Therefore, in the context of the mutual dependence of object and definition, how can impermanence exist depending on the existence of the object? Therefore, existence itself is designated in dependence. Thus, if non-existence were nirvana, how could it be nirvana without dependence? It would have to be dependent, because it is non-existence, just like destruction. He clarifies this: "For there is no non-existence that exists without dependence."

If, then, non-existence does not exist without dependence, will things like the son of a barren woman be non-existences depending on something? Who said that the son of a barren woman is a non-existence? It was said before:

> If existence is not established, non-existence is not established.
> People speak of non-existence as the transformation of existence.
-> [MMK 15.5] <-

Therefore, the son of a barren woman does not have the nature of non-existence. And regarding what is said:

> Space, a rabbit's horn, and the son of a barren woman
> Are spoken of as non-existents; similarly, there is conceptualization in existents.
-> [Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra 2.166, 10.453] <-

In that case, too, it is only a refutation of the conceptualization of existence, not an affirmation of the conceptualization of non-existence, for the very existence of the entity is not established. "Son of a barren woman" is merely a word; no object is found, so it cannot be said to be either existence or non-existence. How can one logically conceive of existence or non-existence for an entity whose nature is not found? Therefore, it should be understood that the son of a barren woman is not a non-existence. Thus, it remains that there is no non-existence that exists without dependence. [8]

Here one asks: If nirvana is not existence, and also not non-existence, then what is nirvana? It is said: Here, the Blessed Tathāgatas have said:

> That which is the cycle of coming and going, when depending or conditioning,
> That, without depending and without conditioning, is taught as nirvana. [9]

"Cycle of coming and going" means the series of births and deaths. This cycle is sometimes designated as existing by relying on a collection of causes and conditions, like "long" or "short." Sometimes it is designated as arising, like the effect of a lamp,

<summary>This page discusses the dependence of all phenomena, including non-existence, and concludes that nirvana is defined as the cessation of the cycle of coming and going without dependence or conditioning.</summary>

while acknowledging that the first signs of that faith are to be found in As'vaghosha's treatise, yet make Nāgārjuna the first in their list of Patriarchs.¹

There is a great deal of uncertainty about As'vaghosha's life. His advent is said to have been foretold by Buddha himself, but Suzuki,² who has written a very full and candid account of As'vaghosha, quotes a passage from a book claiming to be written by Nāgārjuna, in which it is stated that, in order to fulfil all the prophecies concerning him, there must have been six As'vaghoshas, each of whom “appeared to fulfil his mission according to the necessity of the time, and there is no contradiction in them.” (Nāgārjuna's book was translated into Chinese in A.D. 401.) According to the first of these prophecies, As'vaghosha had been a disciple of Buddha in his earthly life. When the Buddha was telling his disciples of his approaching Nirvana, he had asked to accompany him, and then, “gazing at the pupil of Buddha's eye, had passed out of life.” In the next prophecy, Buddha is said to have told As'vaghosha that *three hundred* years after the Nirvana, he would obtain an inspiration from him which would be for the happiness of mankind. According to another, he was to come *six hundred* years after the Nirvana to confute the heretics. A fourth prophecy places him in the *eighth century* after the Nirvana; a fifth brings him back to *one hundred* years. A sixth represents him as having appeared to Buddha, seventeen days after his Enlightenment, in the form of a monster serpent with 86,000 heads and 86,000 tongues, and to have asked the Tathāgata 86,000 questions all at once. This sixth legend was evidently invented to bolster up the pretended revelations of the Kegon Scrip-

We read in the *Brihadâranyaka Upanishad* (II, 3): "Two forms of Brahman there are indeed, the material and the immaterial, the mortal and the immortal, the solid and the fluid, sat and tya." The text then divides the five elements into two classes, attributes qualities like "saffron-color" to the essence of the immaterial (which it calls <term>purusha</term>), and then says: "Now then the teaching by 'Not so, not so!' For there is nothing else higher than this (if one says): It is not so." 

We must inquire what the object of this negative statement is. We do not see any specific thing indicated by words like "this" or "that." We only have the word "so" in "Not so, not so!" to which the word "not" refers, indicating something meant to be denied. The word "so" is used here for proximate things, similar to the particle "thus"; for example, "Thus the teacher said." In our passage, the context points to the two cosmic forms of Brahman, and Brahman itself, as the proximate objects.

A doubt arises: does "Not so, not so!" deny both Brahman and its two forms, or only one? If the latter, does it deny Brahman while leaving the forms, or deny the forms while leaving Brahman? The <term>pûrvapakshin</term> <note>The opponent representing the opposing view.</note> suggests that the negative statement denies both Brahman and its forms, as both are suggested by the context. Since "not" is repeated twice, there are two negative statements: one denying the cosmic form of Brahman, the other denying the entity that has form—that is, Brahman itself. Alternatively, perhaps only Brahman is negated, because Brahman transcends all speech and thought, making its existence questionable, whereas the cosmic forms fall within the sphere of perception and cannot be negated. In this second view, the repetition of "not" is merely for emphasis.

<summary>The author introduces the "Not so, not so" (Neti, neti) passage from the Brihadâranyaka Upanishad and outlines the debate over whether this negation applies to Brahman, its forms, or both.</summary>

In the same way as sleep and the like, the departure of the soul is only referred to in the texts as something established elsewhere (not as something to be taught as part of true knowledge). Passages such as ‘When a man sleeps,—is hungry,—is thirsty’ (*Kh*. Up. VI, 8), although forming part of chapters concerned with true knowledge, mention sleep and so on which are common to all living beings, because they assist the comprehension of the matter to be taught, but do not aim at enjoining them specially for those who know. Analogously the texts about the soul’s departure refer to that departure only in order to teach that ‘that highest deity in which the heat of the dying man is merged, that is the Self, that art thou.’ Now that departure is (in other scriptural passages) specially denied of him who knows; it therefore belongs to him only who does not know.

To this we make the following reply. That departure which is described in the passage, ‘speech is merged in mind,’ &c., must be ‘common’ to him who knows and him who does not know ‘up to the beginning of the way;’ because scripture records no distinction. The soul destitute of true knowledge having taken its abode in the subtle elements which constitute the seed of the body and being impelled by its works, migrates into a new body; while the soul of him who knows passes into the vein, revealed by true knowledge, which is the door of release. In this sense the Sûtra says ‘up to the beginning of the way.’—But he who knows reaches immortality, and immortality does not depend on a change of place; why then should the soul take its abode in the elements or set out on a journey?—That immortality, we reply, is ‘without having burned,’ i. e. for him who, without having altogether burned nescience and the other afflictions, is about to obtain, through the power of the lower knowledge, a relative immortality only, there take place the entering on the way and the abiding in the elements. For without a substratum the prâṇas could not move. There is thus no difficulty.

The word 'also' supplies the further reason why Kṛṣṇa Vâsudeva is to be worshipped, viz., the recollection in the Smṛti that the devotees of Kṛṣṇa have also attained the fruit of immortality.—27

If you ask, why then has Vâsudeva been celebrated as one of the vibhûtis, the author replies.

**वृष्णिषु श्रेष्ठ्येन तत् ॥ २ । १ । २८ ॥**

वृष्णिषु Vṛṣṇiṣu, among the Vṛṣṇis. श्रेष्ठ्येन Śraiṣṭhyena, by reason of superiority, pre-eminence तत् Tat, that i. e. celebration among the vibhûtis.

28 His celebration as a vibhûti is by virtue of his pre-eminence.—54.

The declaration of the vibhûtis is solely for the purpose of opening the eyes of the reader to the fact that it is to the Supreme Lord to Whom belongs all pre-eminence mentioned in such passages as 'Among the Âdityas I am Viṣṇu' (Gîtâ, x, 21), etc.; and so too in the case of Vâsudeva: also, the celebration of Vâsudeva among the vibhûtis is for the purpose of opening the eyes of the reader to this fact only that He is the most excellent one among the Vṛṣṇis.—28.

**एवं प्रसिद्धेषु च ॥ २ । १ । २९ ॥**

एवं Evam, similarly. प्रसिद्धेषु Prasiddheṣu, in regard to well-known incarnations च Cha, and.

29. And similarly in regard to well-known incarnations.—55.

'Similarly,' i. e. in the same way as in the case of Vâsudeva, it should be understood that devotion to the other well-known incarnations such as Varâha, Nṛsiṃha, Vâmana, Râma, etc. also produces mukti as its fruit owing to these incarnations possessing the characteristic mark of Brahman. Or, the aphorism may mean that 'similarly,' i. e., by means of their possessing the characteristic mark of Brahman, the idea of excellence only is to be formed in regard to the objects which have been recited as vibhûtis in such passages as 'Among the Rudras I am Śaṅkara' (Gîtâ, x, 23) etc. For it is declared in the Skanda Purâṇa (Kâśikhaṇḍa, Pûrvabhâga, xxxvii, 181).

"Whoever would declare the difference of Viṣṇu and Rudra, or between Śrî and Gaurî,
That utterance of the erring fool is repugnant to the Śâstra"

The proof of Śaṅkara's possessing the characteristic mark of Brahman is abundantly found in the Smṛti, etc.—29

Thus ends the first lecture of the second chapter in the Commentary on the One Hundred Aphorisms of Sâṇḍilya composed by the most learned teacher Svapneśvara.

भक्त्याहमेकया ग्राह्यः श्रद्धयात्मा प्रियः सताम् ।
भक्तिः पुनाति मन्निष्ठा श्वपाकानपि सम्भवात् ॥ ८६ ॥
( ११ । १४ । १९-२१ श्रीकृष्ण )

किञ्च भक्तस्य प्रायश्चित्तान्तरापेक्षापि नास्तीत्याह यथेति । पाकाद्यर्थं प्रज्वलितो वह्निः यथा काष्ठानि भस्मीकरोति तथा रागादिवासनापि कथञ्चित् मन्निष्ठा सती भक्तिः ॥ ८७ ॥

समस्तपापानीति । भगवानपि स्वभक्तिमहिमाश्चर्येण सशोधयति । अहो उद्धवति अत एवभूत श्रेयो नास्त्यन्यदित्याह न साधयतीति । न साधयतीति न वशीकरोति यथा भक्तिः साधयति अतएव ऊर्जिता योगादिभ्य उत्कृष्टा ॥ ८८ ॥

सर्वपावनत्वाच्चोर्जितेत्याह भक्त्येति श्रद्धया भक्ति तया । सम्भवात् जातिदोषादपि यत्र मद्भक्तो जातिचाण्डालत्वं जहाति तत्र कर्मचाण्डालत्वं जहातीति भावम् ॥ ८९ ॥

87-89 As the fire with its briskly kindled flames reduces fuel to ashes so does, O Uddhava, devotion to me consume all sins. Neither Yoga (Karma-yoga) nor Sânkhya (Jnâna yoga), nor the practice of ordinances (Vedic ritualistic rites) nor recitation of the Vedas, performance of penances nor deeds of charity wins me so much O Uddhava, as does devotion which is superior to all. Only one pointed devotion and faith am I won. I who am the very loved life of the saints. Devotion to me sanctifies even the feeder on dog's flesh (the Chândala the lowest of the social strata) and purifies him of the stain of his birth and vocation — XI 14 19-21 (Kṛṣṇa)

Note — Instances of members of the most depressed classes having been elevated into the rank of saints occur in the religious, especially Vaishnava, literature of the Hindus.

धर्म सत्यदयोपेतो विद्या वा तपसान्विता ।
मद्भक्त्या चेतसात्मानं न सम्यक् प्रपुनाति हि ॥ ९० ॥
( ११ । १४ । २२ श्रीकृष्ण )

Note — This may be a hit against the atheistic Bauddhas and Jainas whose systems of religion differ so much in essentials from the theistic Bhâgavatas.

It does not win Him over like devotion does, therefore it is "superior" to Yoga and the like.—87-88.

Because it is universally purifying, it is called "superior." By devotion and faith, one is won. By birth, even if a devotee is a <term>Châṇḍâla</term> <gloss>the lowest of the social strata; an outcaste</gloss>, he abandons the stain of his birth. Only by one-pointed devotion and faith am I won; I who am the very loved life of the saints. Devotion to me sanctifies even the feeder on dog's flesh and purifies him of the stain of his birth and vocation.—XI. 14. 19-21 (Kṛiṣṇa)

In two verses, the text explains that without devotion, other means are useless even if one is established in them. Religion, learning, or knowledge of the self purifies the heart, but not thoroughly or completely.—90.

How can the heart be purified without devotion, without the hair standing on end <note>a sign of ecstatic devotion</note>, without a melting heart, and without the flow of tears of joy?—91.

ननु आत्मधधनात् धरान्तर मा वृणीत मोक्षेण किमपराद्धमिति चेत् न तत्पादसेवारसिकस्य तद्विरोधेषु विपयेष्विव तच्छून्ये मोक्षादपि वैराग्योचित्या दित्याह द्वाभ्याम् भोक्तृणपद्माख्यायेन । न वयमिति । हे सखि द्रौपदि साम्राज्य सार्वभौमपद स्वाराज्य पेद्र पद भोज्य तदुभयभोगमार्क । विधिवेन राजत इति विराड् तस्य भावो वैराज्य अणिमादिद्धिमाकमित्यर्थ । पारमेष्ठ्य ब्रह्मपदं आनन्त्य मोक्ष हरे पद तत्सालोफ्यं नतु कामयामहे । यद्वा पूर्वादि दिक्चतुष्टयाधिपत्य साम्राज्यादि चतुष्कम् । कितु एतस्य गदाभृत श्रीमत्सर्वसपदाभयपादरजे। मूर्ध्ना वोढु कामयामहे । तत्सेवामेव वञ्छाम इत्यर्थ । तत्कि पादरज एव काम्यते अत आह । भ्रिय कुचयो कुकुमस्य गधेन आद्य ब्रह्मदिसेव्यया श्रियापि सेवितत्वात् इति भाव ॥ २२-२३ ॥

> 22-23 We do not, O virtuous lady, desire for the sovereignty of the earth, or of the heavens, of the regions of Brahma, of Patal or even Moksa. But we do desire to have the blessed dust of the foot of the discus-holder (Narayana), the dust which is fragrant with the saffron of Laksmi's bosom — X 83 41-42 (The Queens to Draupadi)

को नु राजन्द्रियवान् मुकुदचरणाबुजम् ।
न भजेत्सर्वतो मृत्युरुपास्यममरोत्तमै ॥ २४ ॥

(११ । २ । ३ शुकः ।)

तस्मात्फलितमाह । शुकचाफ्येन को नु राजन्निति । हे राजन् परीक्षित इन्द्रियवान् अधिकलेंद्रिय । सर्वतो मृत्यु भय यस्य स । मुकुदचरणाम्बुज भजेत तस्यैव अभयत्वादिति भाव ॥ २४ ॥

24 O King (Pariksit) ! what person, that is in possession of his sense, would not worship the foot of Mukunda, adored by the greatest gods? Surrounded as that man is by Terror (Death) — XI 2 2 (Suka)

मन्ये कुतश्चिद्भयमच्युतस्य पादाम्बुजोपासनमत्र नित्यम् ।
उद्विग्नबुद्धेरसदात्मभावाद्विश्वात्मना यत्र निवर्तते भी ॥ २५ ॥

(११ । २ । ३३ कवि )

एतदेव कविवाक्येनाह । मन्य इति । न कुतश्चिद्भय यस्य तदकुतश्चिद्भयं तव अत्र संसारे असदात्मभावात् असति देहादौ आत्मभावात् भावनात् नित्य सर्वदा उद्विग्नबुद्धे विश्वात्मना सर्वथा निःशेष यत्र पदायुजोपासने भी निवर्तते तत् । तस्मात्स्वधर्मत्यागेनापि भगवत्पादसेवन कार्यमिति रहस्यम् ॥ २५ ॥

25 I consider that the worship of Achyuta (Visnu) should be the unceasing duty of man in this world. For distracted by divergent thoughts he identifies his spirit with his body. He gets rid of his fears by so doing (i.e., by his devotion to Visnu) — XI 2 33 (Kavi)

<term>na vayaṃ sādhiṣa sāmrajyaṃ svarājyaṃ bhojyamapyuta |</term>
<term>vairājyaṃ pārameṣṭhyaṃ vā ānantyaṃ vā hareḥ padam || 22 ||</term>
<term>kāmayāmahe etasya śrīmatpādarajaḥ śriyaḥ |</term>
<term>kucakuṅkumagandhāḍhyaṃ mūrdhnā voḍhuṃ gadābhṛtaḥ || 23 ||</term>
(X. 83. 41-42. The Queens)

<note>The Queens of <term>Krishna</term> address <term>Draupadi</term>, explaining that they do not seek the sovereignty of the earth, the heavens, or the status of <term>Brahmâ</term> or <term>Pâtâla</term>. They only desire the dust from the feet of the Lord (<term>Gadābhṛta</term>—the discus-holder), which is fragrant with the saffron of <term>Lakṣmī's</term> bosom, to place upon their heads.</note>

22-23. We do not, O virtuous lady, desire for the sovereignty of the earth, or of the heavens, of the regions of <term>Brahmâ</term>, of <term>Pâtâla</term>, or even <term>Mokṣa</term>. But we do desire to have the blessed dust of the foot of the discus-holder (<term>Nârâyana</term>), the dust which is fragrant with the saffron of <term>Lakṣmī's</term> bosom — X. 83. 41-42 (The Queens to Draupadi).

<term>ko nu rājannindriyavān mukundacaraṇābujam |</term>
<term>na bhajetsarvato mṛtyurupāsyamamarottamaiḥ || 24 ||</term>
(XI. 2. 3. Suka)

24. O King (<term>Parīkṣit</term>)! what person that is in possession of his senses would not worship the foot of <term>Mukunda</term>, adored by the greatest gods? Surrounded as that man is by Terror (Death) — XI. 2. 3 (Suka).

<term>manye kutaścidbhayamacyutasya pādāmbujopāsanamatra nityam |</term>
<term>udvignabuddherasadātmabhāvādviśvātmanā yatra nivartate bhī || 25 ||</term>
(XI. 2. 33. Kavi)

25. I consider that the worship of <term>Achyuta</term> (<term>Viṣṇu</term>) should be the unceasing duty of man in this world. For distracted by divergent thoughts, he identifies his spirit with his body. He gets rid of his fears by so doing (i.e., by his devotion to <term>Viṣṇu</term>) — XI. 2. 33 (Kavi).

<summary>This page illustrates the surrender of the Queens to the Lord's feet and reinforces the necessity of devotion as a protection against the fear of death and bodily identification.</summary>
